title: Least-frequently-used cache
prompt:
Design a fixed-capacity key-value cache that evicts the least frequently used key, breaking ties by least recent use, with O(1) get and put.

- Implement the class LfuCache(capacity) with get(key) and put(key, value). The driver runLfuCache(capacity, ops) is already written: ops looks like [["put", 1, 10], ["get", 1]] and it returns one output per op (null/None for "put").
- Each key has a use count. A new key starts at 1. A successful get, or a put that overwrites an existing key, adds 1 and also counts as the key's most recent use.
- get(key) returns the value, or -1 if the key is absent (a miss changes nothing).
- put of a new key when the cache already holds capacity keys first evicts the key with the smallest use count; among those, the one whose most recent use is oldest. Evicted keys lose their count.
- capacity is 1 to 10,000; keys are integers; values are integers from 0 to 10^9; up to 100,000 ops.
hints: A heap keyed by (count, last use) works in O(log n). To reach O(1), notice that a key's count only ever goes up by exactly one.
Group keys by use count: a map from count to an ordered set of keys (oldest use first), plus a map from key to (value, count). Track the smallest count that has keys.

On a use, move the key from bucket f to the end of bucket f + 1; if bucket f became empty and f was the minimum, the minimum becomes f + 1. On insert, evict the first key of the minimum bucket if full, add the new key to bucket 1, and set the minimum to 1.

solution.explanation: Keys are grouped into buckets by use count, and each bucket is an insertion-ordered set so its oldest key sits at the front. A use moves a key from bucket f to the back of bucket f + 1; the smallest non-empty count is tracked in minFreq, which can only grow by one on a use and resets to 1 on every insert. Eviction removes the front key of bucket minFreq, so every operation is O(1).

complexity.notes: Ordered sets come from Set (JavaScript) and OrderedDict (Python); by hand each bucket is a doubly linked list. Average O(1) because the maps are hash tables.

followUps: Add frequency decay: halve every count after each 1,000 operations. What breaks in the O(1) design?
When would LFU beat LRU in practice, and when does it behave badly (for example, after a traffic shift)?
